title: New review launched of Vancouver police officers' conduct in controversial 2015 death of Myles Gray
subtitle: The OPCC is taking another look at earlier disciplinary proceedings that found seven officers did not commit misconduct
article: The Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner is taking a new look at the outcome of a discipline proceeding into the 2015 death of Myles Gray during a violent struggle with Vancouver police officers.

A police discipline authority found the seven officers involved did not commit misconduct in Gray's death. While the office doesn't have the authority to rule on police misconduct, it can investigate police actions "in the public interest to ensure allegations are fully investigated and fairly decided."

In a statement Thursday, the office said it will decide whether to arrange a further review by a retired judge, and make recommendations "to address any concerns arising from the actions of the police officers or about the disciplinary process more generally."

The office started an investigation under the Police Act less than a week after Gray's death on Aug. 13, 2015. The process was suspended while the death was investigated by the Independent Investigations Office into whether the actions of the officers were potentially criminal.

In 2020, the B.C. Prosecution Service announced it would not lay criminal charges. In early 2021, the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner resumed its investigation, which was conducted by the RCMP.
That led to a discipline proceeding, convened in March 2023 and held before Chief Const. Neil Dubord of the Delta Police Department as the designated discipline authority.

A coroner's inquest into Gray's death wrapped up in May 2023. The jury's verdict classified Gray's death as a homicide and made recommendations about body cameras, crisis de-escalation training and the retention of evidence.

The Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner discipline proceeding, which took about 19 months to complete, was closed to the public. The only participants were the officers and Dubord. That led to a ruling that no officers committed misconduct, and that allegations of abuse of authority related to the use of force and neglect of duty due to inadequate documentation by the officers were not proven.

The office "appreciates the significant toll this process has had on the family and all parties involved," said the statement. "We will be carefully reviewing the outcome of the discipline proceeding and the process which led us here and will release further information to the public once this review has been completed.
"We have an obligation to the residents of B.C. to ensure there is a fair and impartial police accountability system."
What is the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner?

The commissioner is a civilian, independent officer of the B.C. legislature that oversees complaints against municipal police in the province. It doesn't investigate or adjudicate misconduct allegations, "but rather acts in the public interest to ensure allegations are fully investigated and fairly adjudicated according to the Police Act and administrative law principles."

An investigation is mandatory whenever death or serious harm results from an incident involving municipal police or when someone was in police care or custody. It is separate and distinct from Independent Investigations Office investigations and is not restricted to evidence gathered by that agency.

It can refer certain types of cases to retired judges for further adjudication, call public hearings and make recommendations to police boards or government about policies, practices or systemic issues that may contribute to misconduct.
